title: Storage Governance Lab: Conditional Ejection Review - Northcove Retail
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a lab-style demo focused on conditional ejection and field-level routing for request logs. Customer cares about avoiding storage of PII, doing selective ejection for high-risk sessions, and having a compact UI to set policies. SE showed API flags and Console toggles; discussion covered auditability (SOC2), KMS integration, and cost tradeoffs between ephemeral storage and short-term retention for debugging.
action_items: Carlos Rivera | Run baseline bench: 2k requests with their prompt set + show difference with prefix caching on/off | 2029-11-19
Maya Chen | Share redaction playbook + security pack (SOC2 summary, KMS integration doc, audit log samples) | 2029-11-15
Adriana Malik | Provide a sample of 100 typical request payloads (anonymized) and the PII fields to treat as sensitive | 2029-11-16
next_steps: Schedule Dedicated sizing call (private deployment options) with infra team
Send console sandbox link with preloaded policy templates (conditional-eject + field-redact)
SE to run requested bench and share latency/cost delta report
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-11-12 | Start: 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Adriana Malik (Northcove Head of Data), Evan Zhou (Northcove DevOps), Priya Nair (Northcove Security)
Links referenced: redaction-playbook.pdf (shared), console-sandbox (link), bench-template.csv (shared)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm maya, AE on the northcove account. carlos will take most of the demo. Adriana, Priya, Evan — thanks for making time.
[00:12] Adriana: Thanks, yeah we are really trying to nail down the storage story. we saw some of the high-level docs but want to walk through a real lab — especially conditional ejection, because we can't persist PII beyond 24 hours in certain flows.
[00:25] Carlos: Great, that's exactly what we're going to show. quick agenda: one, how the API flags work for request_storage / telemetry.capture; two, console policy builder for field-level routing and ejection; three, short live lab with sample payloads; four, Q&A on security and logging.
[00:40] Evan: sounds good. Also, can you show how this ties to KMS keys? auditing is big for us.
[00:46] Carlos: absolutely — we'll show how audit logs persist and how encryption-at-rest uses customer-managed keys in the private deployment paths. keep in mind that hosted API also supports envelope encryption with our KMS or your HSM via the Private plane.
[00:58] Maya: small ask — Priya wanted to see how we handle field detection for unstructured prompts, e.g., credit card numbers inside a user message.
[01:06] Priya: yes this, and also 'what happens if detection is wrong' — we need both preventative controls and post-hoc ejection.
[01:13] Carlos: good callout. two layers: automatic PII detectors that run inline and can redact before storage, and a conditional ejection policy that will mark an entire request session for immediate ejection from ephemeral caches and not persist to long-term telemetry.
[01:25] Carlos: switching to the console — here is the policy builder. you can say: if message contains 'ssn' pattern OR high-confidence cc number, then set request_storage = ephemeral and set telemetry.capture = minimal. we also support label-based routing, so you can tie a user cohort to a routing tier that always uses ephemeral mode.
[01:48] Adriana: is this rule language regex-based or ML-based? how do we configure false positive thresholds?
[01:54] Carlos: it's both — we offer regex & ML detectors. regex is immediate for strict formats; ML detector looks for context. threshold is configurable per rule; by default we favor recall for safety but you can tune it to precision if you want fewer false positives.
[02:10] Evan: when you say 'ephemeral' does it completely avoid disk? we need to ensure some telemetry for debugging but only for X hours.
[02:18] Carlos: ephemeral means we do not write to the long-term request store. we may keep encrypted in-memory or short-lived KV cache for the duration of the session (configurable TTL: e.g., 30s, 10m, 24h). if you need debugging, you can enable 'store-for' minutes on a per-request basis. so tradeoff: ephemeral === lower risk, but harder to debug unless you snapshot.
[02:38] Priya: okay and the audit trail? we need records showing that a request was ejected, who triggered it and timestamp.
[02:45] Carlos: audit logs are separate — every decision (rule matched, ejection performed) emits an audit entry with hash of the request id. content is redacted in logs per policy, but you get metadata: request_id, rule_id, action, user, timestamp. those logs are immutable and can be shipped to your SIEM.
[03:01] Maya: quick demo: i'll toggle an inline policy. note — this is sandbox environment with the policy preloaded.
[03:08] Carlos: showing the API flag example: POST /v1/generate with header X-Redwood-Request-Storage: ephemeral or X-Redwood-Request-Storage: store-for=1440 to store for 24h. we also have telemetry.capture=minimal|full.
[03:26] Evan: is the header enforced server-side or can users spoof it?
[03:29] Carlos: authenticated clients can propose flags, but policies may override them. for example, if your global policy mandates ephemeral for the 'payments' route, any incoming header will be overridden. client headers are advisory unless allowed by policy.
[03:42] Adriana: can we tie policy to route+token+workspace? we want different teams to have different defaults.
[03:48] Carlos: yes, policy scope supports route, token, workspace, and label. you can nest policies and set inheritance. default stacks up and the most restrictive wins unless you explicitly allow a less restrictive override.
[04:05] Priya: about KMS — are keys per-tenant? how do we do key rotation?
[04:10] Carlos: in Private you can bring your own key (BYOK) and rotate via the API. rotations create new envelope keys and we keep a key history for decrypting older telemetry for audits. all of this is logged to the audit bucket.
[04:23] Maya: ok quick lab — carlos will paste three sample requests, one benign, one with a simulated credit card string, one with a PII name pattern.
[04:31] Carlos: pasting request 1. [04:35] — console shows matched rules: none. request storage = store-for=1440.
[04:40] Carlos: request 2 pasted. [04:44] — ML detector flag high confidence 'cc' pattern; action: redact detected tokens and set request_storage=ephemeral; audit event created.
[04:50] Priya: I see the redacted preview. it's not perfect — masked with **** — is that reversible?
[04:55] Carlos: by design redaction is irreversible in the hosted flow. in Private we can offer reversible tokenization under your HSM but that requires strict access controls and audit approvals.
[05:05] Adriana: hmm for our use case, irreversible redaction is preferred for most data, but we occasionally need reversible for fraud investigations. how would that work?
[05:13] Carlos: we recommend doing reversible for a limited subset: route-isolation + RBAC so only a small operations group can request unredaction and that action is logged. that requires Private deployment with BYOK and HSM-backed token vault.
[05:27] Evan: latency questions — what hit do we see when detectors run inline?
[05:31] Carlos: depends. regex checks are ~2-5ms. ML detector ranges 12-40ms depending on length — we run optimized models on the runtime with batching where possible. for strict low-latency SLAs, use the console to pre-populate allowlists or route certain traffic to a lower-sensitivity path.
[05:50] Maya: we should also mention Optimize suggestions — if you enable prefix caching or change batch size, you reduce token compute cost; Optimize will propose quantized model variants for non-sensitive traffic.
[06:03] Adriana: can Optimize recommendations be limited to non-PII routes? we don't want cheaper quantized models touching sensitive inputs.
[06:09] Carlos: yes, policy prevents model variants from being selected for routes marked 'sensitive'. Optimize suggestions are annotated with compliance tags so the operator can accept or reject per route.
[06:20] Evan: walk me through an incident: a developer accidentally sends real PII in a test route flagged ephemeral. what's the rollback / ejection flow?
[06:28] Carlos: three steps: 1) policy triggers ejection — request not persisted; 2) audit log created; 3) if you have configured immediate ejection to downstream stores, we also remove cached KV entries. if the data escaped to third-party telemetry, that's a different chain — but Redwood can send notifications and construct an evidence packet.
[06:45] Priya: okay good. any limits on audit retention for regulatory reasons? our retention policy needs 7 years for certain records, but only metadata, not the PII itself.
[06:55] Carlos: audit metadata retention is separate from request content. you can specify retention windows per audit bucket; in Private deployments you can set up S3 lifecycle or your archival store. hosted has presets and a configurable SLA for longer retention as an add-on.
[07:10] Maya: quick question from SRE perspective: will ejection cause higher CPU if we do mass deletes?
[07:16] Carlos: deletes are async and use tombstoning plus compaction. mass ejections are batched to avoid spikes. we can also offload compaction to maintenance windows in Dedicated clusters.
[07:29] Adriana: is there a way to preview the policy impact before turning it on? we don't want a policy that accidentally marks everything ephemeral.
[07:36] Carlos: yes — policy dry-run mode. you can run historical replay on a sample of logs to see match rates and estimated false positives. we show a heatmap of matches by route so you can tune thresholds.
[07:49] Evan: can dry-run replay be run on customer data in-place? we need to preserve privacy during that analysis.
[07:55] Carlos: dry-run can be run on anonymized snapshots or via a privacy-preserving mode where we hash sensitive tokens before evaluation. we also support a synthetic replay mode using synthetic data generated to match distribution.
[08:08] Priya: on the console, where do we set TTLs? route-level or policy-level?
[08:12] Carlos: both. you get defaults at account level, route overrides, and per-request flags. the precedence: per-request header -> route override -> account default -> global default. safety policies can lock precedence.
[08:26] Maya: time check — about 30 minutes in. any urgent questions?
[08:31] Adriana: only one: cost delta between short-term store-for=60m vs ephemeral with snapshot-on-demand. we need ballpark numbers.
[08:38] Carlos: rough ballpark: storing for 60m at our hosted rates is about 12% more token cost due to write amplification and retention; snapshot-on-demand can be cheaper but adds storage spikes. we'll run an exact bench for your prompt set in the follow-up.
[08:52] Maya: ok lab wrap-up. i'll recap main points and next steps.
[08:57] Carlos: final note — here's the policy template name 'northcove-conditional-eject-1' shared to the sandbox. you can import and tweak.
[09:06] Priya: good, please include the SOC2 artifact and a note about irreversible redaction vs reversible tokenization.
[09:14] Maya: will do. thanks everyone. we'll send the pack and set up the Dedicated sizing call.
[09:20] Adriana: thanks all.

End of transcript.
